title: Short Stuff: The Paper Dress Fad
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the mid-1960s paper dress fad. Scott Paper Company created paper dresses (made of Dura-weave, a paper and rayon material) as a marketing stunt for its durable product, offering them for a small fee after customers mailed in proof of purchase. The dresses, including the red bandana and black-and-white op art designs, took off, prompting Scott to advertise in magazines like Mademoiselle, and other companies followed with designs such as Waste Basket Boutique's line, with pop art, celebrity, and food-themed prints. The hosts discuss why the fad took off (plastic and disposability trends, pop and op art, sexual revolution, new-style freedom), hotel chains' ideas for paper clothing, and why it faded (mini dress going out of style, discomfort and wrinkling, environmental consciousness after Earth Day 1970, and the fact that replacement clothing is also disposable).

segments.title: Introduction and origins of the paper dress
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic. Scott Paper Company's Dura-weave, a paper and rayon product, was promoted by making paper dresses; customers mailed in a clip and a dollar plus a quarter to receive a red bandana or black-and-white op art dress. The response was huge and Scott advertised in magazines such as Mademoiselle.

segments.title: Why the fad took off and early production
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Scott sold the dresses cheaply and barely broke even. Other companies saw profit potential, and the dresses matched 1960s plastic, disposable, and pop culture trends. Roughly three and a half million dollars' worth of paper garments sold, and Waste Basket Boutique reportedly made a hundred thousand a week.

segments.title: Designs, prints, and benefits of paper dresses
segments.summary: Paper was easy to print on, so designers made many lines with pop art and op art prints, including Campbell soup, Jolly Green Giant, and candy bar designs, plus celebrity faces such as Bob Dylan, Richard Nixon, and Bobby Kennedy. Young women gained new outfits they could cheaply alter, amid the sexual revolution.

segments.title: Hotel paper clothing idea and other paper garments
segments.summary: The hosts describe a proposal by hotel chains to sell paper clothing in gift shops so guests could avoid packing. The idea did not catch on. Companies also made paper men's suits, and the material was similar to Dura-weave, the same kind used in dental bibs.

segments.title: Why the fad faded
segments.summary: The hosts cite several reasons for the decline: mini dresses fell out of style by 1968 or 1969, Jonathan Walford of the Fashion History Museum said the dresses were uncomfortable and wrinkled, they were prone to spills at parties, and growing environmental awareness around the first Earth Day in 1970. They note that replacement clothing is also disposable.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode with a joke about future paper tuxedos and a sign-off for Short Stuff.
